q: The tube that carries urine from each kidney to the urinary bladder is the:
x: Each kidney drains urine into its own ureter, which carries it to the urinary bladder. The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside.

q: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the:
x: The nephron is the basic unit that filters blood and forms urine. The glomerulus is only one part of the nephron, and a neuron is the unit of the nervous system.

q: The outer, granular region of the kidney lying just beneath the capsule is the:
x: The cortex is the outer region; it looks granular because it contains the renal corpuscles. The medulla lies inside it and the pelvis is the central cavity.

q: Bowman's capsule together with the glomerulus it encloses is called the:
x: The cup-shaped Bowman's capsule and the knot of capillaries inside it (glomerulus) together form the Malpighian body, also called the renal corpuscle.

q: Urine is stored temporarily before it is passed out of the body in the:
x: The muscular urinary bladder stores urine until it is emptied through the urethra. The pelvis and ureter only conduct urine onward.

q: The renal pelvis is best described as:
o: The funnel-shaped expanded upper end of the ureter inside the kidney
The outer granular layer of the kidney
A cone-shaped mass of tubules in the medulla
The cup-shaped beginning of each nephron
x: The renal pelvis is the funnel-like cavity formed by the expanded upper end of the ureter; it collects urine from the collecting ducts. The cup-shaped beginning of a nephron is Bowman's capsule.

q: Where are the human kidneys located?
o: In the pelvic cavity below the urinary bladder
In the thoracic cavity just below the lungs
In front of the stomach, attached to the liver
Against the dorsal wall of the abdomen, one on each side of the vertebral column
x: The two kidneys lie against the back (dorsal) wall of the abdominal cavity, on either side of the vertebral column, behind the peritoneum.

q: The cone-shaped renal pyramids, made mainly of loops of Henle and collecting ducts, are found in the:
x: The medulla is divided into renal pyramids, whose striped look comes from the parallel loops of Henle and collecting ducts. Their tips open towards the renal pelvis.

q: What is the correct path followed by filtrate through a nephron?
o: Bowman's capsule → DCT → loop of Henle → PCT → collecting duct
Bowman's capsule → PCT → loop of Henle → DCT → collecting duct
Glomerulus → loop of Henle → PCT → DCT → collecting duct
Bowman's capsule → PCT → DCT → loop of Henle → collecting duct
x: Filtrate enters Bowman's capsule, then flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle and the distal convoluted tubule before draining into a collecting duct.

q: In a nephron, Bowman's capsule and the proximal and distal convoluted tubules are located in the:
x: The renal corpuscle and both convoluted tubules lie in the cortex. Only the loop of Henle (and the collecting duct) dips down into the medulla.

q: Cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have a brush border of microvilli and many mitochondria. These features suit them mainly for:
o: Storing urine before it reaches the pelvis
Active reabsorption over a large surface area
x: Microvilli give a huge surface area and mitochondria supply ATP, so PCT cells are built for active reabsorption of glucose, amino acids and ions. Filtration happens in the renal corpuscle, not here.

q: The inner layer of Bowman's capsule, which wraps around the glomerular capillaries, is made of specialised cells called:
x: Podocytes have foot-like processes that wrap the glomerular capillaries and leave narrow filtration slits between them. Brush-border cells line the PCT.

q: How do juxtamedullary nephrons differ from cortical nephrons?
o: Their glomeruli lie near the cortex–medulla border and their loops of Henle reach deep into the medulla
They lie entirely in the medulla, including their glomeruli
They open directly into the ureter instead of a collecting duct
x: Juxtamedullary nephrons have glomeruli close to the medulla and long loops of Henle that run deep into it. Cortical nephrons have glomeruli in the outer cortex and short loops.

q: Which type of nephron is mainly responsible for the kidney's ability to produce concentrated urine?
o: Juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops of Henle
Cortical nephrons with short loops of Henle
Nephrons that lack a distal convoluted tubule
Nephrons whose glomeruli lie in the medulla
x: The long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons build up the high salt concentration deep in the medulla, which lets water be drawn out of the collecting ducts to make concentrated urine.

q: The glomerulus is a tuft of many capillaries with a very large total surface area. This feature mainly helps the kidney to:
o: Form a large volume of filtrate quickly
Actively pump glucose back into blood
Produce hormones that control water balance
x: A large filtering surface allows a large volume of filtrate to form every minute. Reabsorption of glucose happens later, in the PCT.

q: Which set of structures passes through the hilum of the kidney?
o: Renal artery, hepatic portal vein and urethra
Renal artery, renal vein and ureter
Aorta, inferior vena cava and ureter
x: The renal artery enters and the renal vein and ureter leave at the hilum, the notch on the inner (concave) side of the kidney. The urethra leaves the bladder, not the kidney.

q: The renal veins carry blood from the kidneys into the:
x: Renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava, which returns blood from the lower body to the heart. The renal arteries branch from the aorta.

q: Which part of the nephron connects the proximal convoluted tubule to the distal convoluted tubule?
x: The U-shaped loop of Henle runs from the PCT down into the medulla and back up to the DCT.

q: The right kidney usually lies slightly lower than the left kidney. This is because of the large organ above it, the:
x: The liver occupies the upper right part of the abdomen, pushing the right kidney a little lower than the left.

q: About how many nephrons are present in each human kidney?
x: Each human kidney contains roughly one million nephrons. The other figures are far too small or far too large.

q: Which pairing of a nephron part with its main role is correct?
o: Proximal convoluted tubule – storage of urine
Collecting duct – formation of glomerular filtrate
Bowman's capsule – active reabsorption of glucose
x: Filtration takes place from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule. Glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT, and urine is stored in the bladder.

q: The cortex of the kidney looks granular, while the medulla looks striped. The stripes of the medulla are due to:
o: Layers of fat around the pelvis
Parallel loops of Henle and collecting ducts
x: In the medulla the loops of Henle and collecting ducts run side by side in the same direction, which gives the pyramids a striated look. The glomeruli make the cortex granular.

q: A nephron has its glomerulus in the outer cortex and a short loop of Henle that barely enters the medulla. Which statement about it is correct?
o: It is a juxtamedullary nephron and makes the most concentrated urine
It has no proximal convoluted tubule
It is a cortical nephron and contributes little to the deep medullary salt gradient
It drains directly into the ureter
x: An outer-cortex glomerulus with a short loop marks a cortical nephron. Because its loop hardly enters the medulla, it adds little to the deep salt gradient that the long juxtamedullary loops build.

q: Desert mammals such as the kangaroo rat have a relatively thick medulla with very long loops of Henle. This mainly allows them to:
o: Filter blood at a much higher rate
Produce very concentrated urine and save water
Store more urine in their kidneys
Excrete uric acid instead of urea
x: Longer loops build a stronger salt gradient in a thicker medulla, so more water can be drawn out of the collecting ducts. The urine becomes highly concentrated and water is conserved.

q: Which statement about the collecting ducts is correct?
o: Each begins at its own Bowman's capsule
They lie entirely within the cortex
They open directly into the urinary bladder
They run from the cortex through the medulla and empty into the renal pelvis
x: Collecting ducts start in the cortex where DCTs join them, pass down through the medullary pyramids and open at the pyramid tips into the renal pelvis.

q: After leaving the collecting ducts, urine passes through which structures, in order?
o: Renal pelvis → urethra → urinary bladder → ureter
Renal pelvis → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra
Urinary bladder → renal pelvis → ureter → urethra
x: Collecting ducts empty into the renal pelvis, which leads into the ureter; the ureter carries urine to the bladder, and the urethra carries it out of the body.

q: All of the following lie in the renal cortex EXCEPT the:
x: Renal pyramids make up the medulla. Glomeruli and both convoluted tubules lie in the cortex.

q: The proximal convoluted tubule is the longest and most coiled part of the nephron. How does this relate to its function?
o: It slows filtration in the glomerulus
It allows urine to be stored in the cortex
It gives a large surface and enough time for most reabsorption to occur
It produces the high pressure needed for filtration
x: A long, coiled tubule with microvilli gives a big surface area and contact time, which suits the PCT for reabsorbing most of the useful substances from the filtrate.

q: Which of these is NOT an organ of the human urinary system?
x: The urinary system is made of the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra. The adrenal gland sits on top of the kidney but is an endocrine gland.

q: Which correctly describes how urine drains within one kidney?
o: Every nephron has its own ureter
Many nephrons drain into each collecting duct, and many collecting ducts empty into one renal pelvis leading to one ureter
Each renal pyramid has its own separate ureter
Each collecting duct serves only one nephron and opens into the bladder
x: Several nephrons share a collecting duct, the ducts open at the pyramid tips into a single renal pelvis, and the pelvis continues as one ureter per kidney.

q: The glomerulus is best described as:
o: A knot of capillaries lying inside Bowman's capsule
The U-shaped part of the tubule in the medulla
The wide cavity at the start of the ureter
x: The glomerulus is a tuft (knot) of blood capillaries enclosed by Bowman's capsule. The cup-shaped sac is the capsule itself.

q: Which part of the nephron receives the glomerular filtrate first?
x: Filtrate is forced out of the glomerular capillaries into the space of Bowman's capsule, and only then flows into the PCT.

q: The first step in the formation of urine is:
o: Water reabsorption in the collecting duct
x: Urine formation starts with filtration of plasma from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule; reabsorption and secretion then modify this filtrate.

q: Which of the following is normally NOT present in glomerular filtrate?
x: Plasma proteins are too large to pass the filtration barrier, so they stay in the blood. Small molecules such as glucose, urea and ions pass into the filtrate.

q: In a healthy person, all the glucose in the filtrate is reabsorbed in the:
x: Glucose (and amino acids) are completely reabsorbed by active transport in the PCT, so normal urine contains no glucose.

q: Glomerular filtration is called ultrafiltration because:
o: Small molecules are forced out of the blood under high pressure through a very fine filter
It uses ATP produced by podocytes
It removes only blood cells from the plasma
It takes place in the loop of Henle
x: Ultrafiltration is filtration under pressure through an extremely fine barrier, which lets water and small solutes through but holds back cells and large proteins.

q: In a glomerulus the blood hydrostatic pressure is 55 mmHg, the osmotic pressure of plasma proteins is 30 mmHg and the hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's capsule is 15 mmHg. The net filtration pressure is:
x: Net filtration pressure = blood pressure minus the opposing forces = 55 − (30 + 15) = 10 mmHg. Forgetting one opposing force gives 25 or 40, and adding all three gives 100.

q: Which force opposes the filtration of fluid out of the glomerular capillaries?
o: Hydrostatic pressure of blood in the glomerulus
The wider diameter of the afferent arteriole
Osmotic pressure due to plasma proteins in the glomerular blood
The pores in the capillary walls
x: Plasma proteins stay in the blood and exert an osmotic pull that draws water back, opposing filtration. Blood hydrostatic pressure is the force that drives filtration.

q: Glucose is reabsorbed from the proximal convoluted tubule mainly by:
x: Glucose is taken back by carrier proteins using energy (active transport, coupled to sodium), so it can be reabsorbed completely even against a gradient.

q: Water is reabsorbed from the proximal convoluted tubule by:
x: As salts, glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed, the tubule fluid becomes less concentrated than the surrounding cells, so water follows by osmosis.

q: The descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to water but not very permeable to salts. As filtrate flows down this limb it becomes:
o: More dilute, as salts are pumped out
More concentrated, as water leaves by osmosis
x: Water leaves the descending limb into the salty medulla by osmosis, while most salt stays in, so the filtrate becomes more concentrated towards the bend.

q: Which part of the nephron actively pumps out sodium and chloride ions but is impermeable to water?
o: Descending limb of the loop of Henle
Ascending limb of the loop of Henle
x: The ascending limb moves salt out into the medulla but does not let water follow. This builds the medullary salt gradient. The descending limb, by contrast, is permeable to water.

q: Tubular secretion is the movement of substances:
o: From the filtrate back into the blood
From the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule
From the blood in surrounding capillaries into the tubule fluid
From the collecting duct into the renal pelvis
x: In secretion, substances such as H+, K+ and some drugs are moved from the peritubular blood into the tubule. Movement from filtrate into blood is reabsorption.

q: Which substance is added to the filtrate by tubular secretion?
x: H+ ions are secreted into the tubule (along with K+, ammonia and some drugs). Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed, and plasma proteins are not filtered at all.

q: Secretion of hydrogen ions into the tubule mainly helps the body to:
o: Keep the pH of the blood constant
Make urine alkaline at all times
x: Secreting excess H+ into urine (and reabsorbing bicarbonate) prevents the blood from becoming too acidic, so the kidney helps regulate blood pH.

q: The main role of the countercurrent multiplier in the loop of Henle is to:
o: Filter plasma proteins out of the blood
Pump glucose back into the blood
Build up a high solute concentration in the medulla so that water can be drawn out of the collecting ducts
x: The loop sets up a rising salt concentration deeper into the medulla. Water then leaves the collecting ducts by osmosis into this salty tissue, producing concentrated urine.

q: The loop of Henle is called a countercurrent system because:
o: Blood and filtrate mix inside it
It pumps filtrate back to the glomerulus
Fluid in its two limbs flows in opposite directions
Urine flows through it from the bladder to the kidney
x: Filtrate flows down the descending limb and up the ascending limb, so the two neighbouring streams run in opposite directions; this lets the effect of salt pumping be multiplied along the loop.

q: Roughly what proportion of the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed back into the blood?
x: Almost all of the filtrate, about 99%, is reabsorbed, so only a small volume leaves as urine.

q: About 180 litres of filtrate form each day, yet only about 1.5 litres of urine are passed. This is mainly because:
o: Most filtrate is stored in the bladder
The glomerulus filters only at night
Most water evaporates from the kidney
Most of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed along the tubule and collecting ducts
x: Reabsorption along the nephron and collecting duct returns almost all the filtered water to the blood, leaving a small volume of urine.

q: Which statement about urea in the nephron is correct?
o: It is not filtered at the glomerulus
It is completely reabsorbed in the PCT
It is filtered freely, and part of it diffuses back into the blood while the rest is excreted
It is made inside the loop of Henle
x: Urea is a small molecule that passes freely into the filtrate. Some diffuses back out passively, but much remains and is excreted. Urea is made in the liver, not the kidney.

q: The largest share of the water, sodium and other useful substances in the filtrate is reabsorbed in the:
o: Descending limb of the loop of Henle
x: Most reabsorption, including all glucose and amino acids and most salts and water, happens in the PCT. Later segments fine-tune what is left.

q: In uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, glucose appears in the urine although the PCT is healthy. The reason is that:
o: Glucose is no longer filtered at the glomerulus
Blood glucose is so high that the filtered load exceeds the capacity of the reabsorbing carriers
x: Glucose is reabsorbed by a limited number of carriers. When blood glucose is very high, more glucose is filtered than the carriers can take back, so the excess passes into urine.

q: Red blood cells are normally absent from glomerular filtrate because they:
o: Are too large to pass through the filtration barrier
Are actively reabsorbed in the PCT
Are secreted back into the efferent arteriole
x: Blood cells are much too large to pass through the pores and filtration slits, so they stay in the blood along with the plasma proteins.

q: Selective reabsorption means that:
o: All substances in the filtrate are returned to the blood
Only waste products are returned to the blood
Useful substances are taken back into the blood while most wastes are left in the filtrate
Filtrate is returned to Bowman's capsule
x: It is selective because the tubule reclaims useful materials such as glucose, amino acids, salts and water, while wastes like urea are largely left to be excreted.

q: Compared with blood plasma, the filtrate at the hairpin bend (tip) of a long loop of Henle is:
x: As filtrate moves down the descending limb it loses water to the salty medulla, so at the tip of the loop it is more concentrated (hypertonic) than plasma.

q: The fluid entering the distal convoluted tubule is hypotonic to blood plasma. This is because in the ascending limb:
o: Water is drawn in from the medulla
Salts are pumped out but water cannot follow
Glucose is added to the filtrate
x: The ascending limb removes salts but is impermeable to water, so the fluid leaving it is more dilute than plasma.

q: Which processes take place in the distal convoluted tubule?
o: Ultrafiltration of plasma and podocyte filtering
Complete reabsorption of glucose and amino acids
Reabsorption of sodium ions and secretion of potassium and hydrogen ions
Storage of urine before it enters the ureter
x: The DCT fine-tunes the filtrate: it reabsorbs Na+ (under aldosterone) and secretes K+ and H+, which helps control salt balance and pH. Glucose is reabsorbed earlier, in the PCT.

q: If the ascending limb of the loop of Henle could no longer pump out sodium chloride, the most direct effect would be that:
o: The medullary salt gradient would fall, so less water could be drawn from the collecting ducts and urine would be more dilute
Glucose would appear in the urine
Plasma proteins would enter the filtrate
Filtration in the glomerulus would stop
x: The salt pumped out by the ascending limb creates the medullary gradient. Without it, water would not be pulled out of the collecting ducts, so the urine could not be concentrated.

q: Which substance is present in glomerular filtrate at about the same concentration as in plasma, but is normally absent from urine?
x: Glucose is freely filtered but completely reabsorbed in the PCT, so normal urine contains none. Urea, creatinine and uric acid are wastes excreted in urine.

q: The concentration of urea in urine is many times higher than in glomerular filtrate. This is mainly because:
o: Large amounts of urea are made in the collecting duct
Urea is actively pumped into the filtrate at the glomerulus
Urea is produced in the bladder
Most of the water is reabsorbed while much of the urea remains in the tubule
x: About 99% of the water is reabsorbed, but a large part of the urea stays behind, so the urea in urine becomes highly concentrated.

q: Which match of nephron segment with what leaves the filtrate there is correct?
o: Proximal tubule – plasma proteins, by active transport
Bowman's capsule – glucose, by active transport
x: The descending limb is permeable to water, which leaves by osmosis into the salty medulla. The ascending limb is impermeable to water, proteins are not filtered, and glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT.

q: The energy that drives glomerular filtration comes from:
o: Blood pressure produced by the pumping of the heart
x: Filtration is a passive process: blood pressure, generated by the heart and kept high in the glomerulus, pushes fluid through the filter. No ATP is used by the filter itself.

q: Which three processes, in order, produce urine in a nephron?
o: Tubular secretion, glomerular filtration, selective reabsorption
Selective reabsorption, glomerular filtration, tubular secretion
Glomerular filtration, selective reabsorption, tubular secretion
x: Blood is first filtered in the glomerulus, useful substances are then reabsorbed, and some substances are secreted into the tubule to finish the urine.

q: A drug blocks the carriers that reabsorb glucose in the PCT of a person with normal blood glucose. What would be expected?
o: Glucose would appear in the urine and urine volume would rise
Glucose would stay in the blood and none would be filtered
Plasma proteins would appear in the urine
Urine would become more concentrated and smaller in volume
x: Glucose is still filtered but can no longer be taken back, so it stays in the tubule and is lost in urine. The extra solute holds water in the tubule by osmosis, increasing urine volume.

q: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is also called:
x: ADH is also known as vasopressin. Aldosterone is an adrenal cortex hormone, oxytocin is another posterior pituitary hormone, and renin is a kidney enzyme.

q: Aldosterone, which acts on the kidney, is secreted by the:
x: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid made by the adrenal cortex. The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline, and the posterior pituitary releases ADH.

q: Osmoregulation is the regulation of:
o: The water and salt (solute) balance of body fluids
x: Osmoregulation keeps the water content and solute concentration of body fluids constant. Temperature control is thermoregulation.

q: The main nitrogenous waste removed from the blood by human kidneys is:
x: Urea, made in the liver from excess amino acids, is the main nitrogenous waste in human urine. Uric acid and creatinine are also excreted but in much smaller amounts.

q: ADH acts on the kidney by making which parts more permeable to water?
o: Ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct
x: ADH increases the water permeability of the DCT and collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood.

q: After heavy sweating on a hot day with little drinking, a person's kidneys will:
o: Produce a large volume of dilute urine as ADH falls
Produce a small volume of concentrated urine as ADH rises
x: Water loss raises the blood's osmotic concentration, so more ADH is released. More water is reabsorbed from the collecting ducts and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.

q: A person drinks a large volume of water quickly. What happens next?
o: ADH secretion increases and urine becomes hypertonic
ADH secretion decreases and a large volume of hypotonic urine is produced
Water is stored in the medulla
x: Extra water dilutes the blood, so ADH release falls. The collecting ducts become less permeable to water and a large volume of dilute (hypotonic) urine is passed.

q: The osmoreceptors that detect changes in the osmotic concentration of blood and control ADH release are located in the:
x: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus sense the blood's water level and signal the posterior pituitary to release more or less ADH.

q: Aldosterone acts on the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to:
o: Increase reabsorption of sodium ions and secretion of potassium ions
x: Aldosterone causes more Na+ to be reabsorbed (water follows) and more K+ to be secreted into urine, so it helps control salt balance and blood volume.

q: A person passes very large volumes of dilute urine and is constantly thirsty, although the blood glucose level is normal. The most likely cause is:
x: Without ADH, the collecting ducts stay poorly permeable to water, so much water is lost in dilute urine. This is diabetes insipidus; normal blood glucose rules out diabetes mellitus.

q: Urine is described as hypertonic when it:
o: Has a lower solute concentration than blood plasma
Has a higher solute concentration than blood plasma
x: Hypertonic urine is more concentrated than plasma; it is produced when the body needs to save water. Hypotonic urine is more dilute than plasma.

q: Kidneys are called organs of both excretion and osmoregulation because they:
o: Only remove water from the blood
Store excess salts for later use
Remove nitrogenous wastes and also adjust the water and salts in urine to keep body fluid concentration constant
x: Removing wastes such as urea is excretion, while varying how much water and salt is lost, according to the body's needs, is osmoregulation.

q: Which kidney activity is an excretory role rather than an osmoregulatory one?
o: Reabsorbing more water when ADH is high
Removing urea and creatinine from the blood
Producing dilute urine after drinking a lot
x: Removing nitrogenous wastes like urea and creatinine is excretion. Adjusting water and salt reabsorption is osmoregulation.

q: Drinking alcohol increases the volume of urine because alcohol:
x: Alcohol suppresses ADH release, so less water is reabsorbed from the collecting ducts and more dilute urine is produced.

q: A fall in the blood's sodium level or blood volume leads to increased secretion of:
x: Low Na+ or low blood volume triggers renin release from the kidney, leading to angiotensin and then aldosterone, which increases Na+ reabsorption.

q: Besides controlling water and salts, the kidneys help keep blood pH constant by:
o: Secreting hydrogen ions into the filtrate and reabsorbing bicarbonate ions
Storing carbon dioxide in the medulla
x: When the blood is too acidic, the tubules secrete more H+ into urine and return bicarbonate to the blood, raising blood pH back to normal.

q: As the blood's osmotic concentration returns to normal after ADH release, the secretion of ADH:
x: ADH control works by negative feedback: once the blood's water content is restored, the stimulus is removed and ADH release falls.

q: When ADH is present, water leaves the collecting duct and enters the blood because:
o: The surrounding medullary fluid is hypertonic
The collecting duct actively pumps water out
The filtrate in the collecting duct contains proteins
x: With ADH the duct wall becomes permeable, and water moves by osmosis into the salty, hypertonic medulla, from where it returns to the blood.

q: ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct by:
o: Adding more water channels (aquaporins) to the membranes of duct cells
Making the duct impermeable to urea and water
x: ADH causes water-channel proteins (aquaporins) to be inserted into the membranes of collecting duct cells, so water can pass out by osmosis.

q: Which pair of hormones both act on the distal parts of the nephron to regulate water and salt balance?
x: ADH controls water reabsorption and aldosterone controls Na+ reabsorption, both in the DCT and collecting duct.

q: Besides increasing sodium reabsorption, aldosterone causes the kidneys to excrete more:
x: Aldosterone causes Na+ to be reabsorbed and K+ to be secreted into the filtrate, so more potassium is lost in urine.

q: Eating a very salty meal raises the osmotic concentration of the blood. The kidneys respond, under ADH, by:
o: Excreting more water to dilute the urine
Reabsorbing more water, producing a smaller volume of concentrated urine
Stopping urine production for a day
x: The rise in blood concentration triggers ADH release, so more water is retained and less, more concentrated urine is made, helping bring the blood concentration back down.

q: A patient's blood has a high osmotic concentration, yet the patient passes a large volume of very dilute urine. Which explanation fits?
o: ADH is absent or the collecting ducts do not respond to it
ADH secretion is very high and working normally
This is the normal response to dehydration
x: Normally a concentrated blood would raise ADH and produce concentrated urine. Dilute urine despite this means ADH is missing or the kidney cannot respond to it.

q: After a severe loss of blood, which kidney response would be expected?
o: Less ADH and less aldosterone, producing a large volume of urine
More ADH but no change in sodium handling, producing glucose in urine
No hormone change but faster filtration
More ADH and more aldosterone, producing a small volume of urine
x: Low blood volume stimulates both ADH and aldosterone. Water and sodium are retained, so urine volume falls and blood volume is helped back up.

q: The kidney's ability to produce urine more concentrated than blood depends on which two features working together?
o: A salt gradient in the medulla and ADH-controlled water permeability of the collecting ducts
Aldosterone and the glomerular filtration rate alone
Glucose reabsorption and tubular secretion of H+
x: The loops of Henle build a salty medulla, and ADH lets the collecting ducts release water into it by osmosis. Without either one, concentrated urine cannot be made.

q: Person P drinks two litres of water; person Q drinks nothing while walking in hot sun. Which comparison is correct?
o: P has more ADH and more concentrated urine than Q
Both have the same ADH level and urine concentration
Q produces a larger volume of urine than P
Q has more ADH and more concentrated urine than P
x: Q is losing water, so blood concentration rises, ADH rises and urine becomes concentrated and small in volume. P has extra water, so ADH falls and urine is dilute and plentiful.

q: Urine can be made more concentrated than blood, but never more concentrated than the fluid in the deepest part of the medulla. Why?
o: ADH stops working at high concentrations
The collecting duct actively secretes water into the medulla
Urea cannot pass through the collecting duct
Water leaves the collecting duct only by osmosis, so it can at most reach the concentration of the surrounding medulla
x: Water reabsorption from the collecting duct is passive osmosis into the medulla. Once the urine matches the concentration of the deepest medulla, there is no gradient left to draw out more water.

q: Which waste product is removed mainly by the lungs rather than by the kidneys?
x: Carbon dioxide from respiration is excreted mainly by the lungs. Urea, uric acid and creatinine are nitrogenous wastes removed by the kidneys.

q: The kidneys contribute to homeostasis by keeping which features of the blood nearly constant?
o: Red cell count, platelet count and haemoglobin
Water content, salt concentration and pH
Blood glucose and insulin level only
x: By adjusting how much water, salts and H+ ions are excreted, the kidneys keep the blood's water content, salt concentration and pH steady.

q: Which statement about ADH is correct?
o: It is made in the adrenal cortex
It increases the reabsorption of sodium in the PCT
It is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary
It causes the production of a large volume of dilute urine
x: ADH is made by neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus and stored in and released from the posterior pituitary. It causes water retention, giving concentrated urine.

q: A tumour of the adrenal cortex secretes too much aldosterone. Which combination is expected?
o: Sodium loss in urine and low blood pressure
Glucose in the urine and high blood potassium
Very dilute urine and low blood volume
Sodium and water retention, raised blood pressure and low blood potassium
x: Excess aldosterone makes the kidney keep more Na+ (water follows, raising blood volume and pressure) and lose more K+, so blood potassium falls.

q: Blood enters the glomerulus through the:
x: The afferent arteriole, a branch of the renal artery system, brings blood into the glomerulus. The efferent arteriole carries it out.

q: Blood leaves the glomerulus through the:
x: Blood that has been filtered leaves the glomerulus through the efferent arteriole, not through a venule.

q: The peritubular capillaries arise from the:
x: The efferent arteriole leaving the glomerulus branches to form the peritubular capillary network around the tubules.

q: The vasa recta are long capillary loops that run alongside the loops of Henle of which nephrons?
o: Nephrons with no loop of Henle
x: Vasa recta come from the efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons and dip deep into the medulla beside their long loops of Henle.

q: Blood pressure in the glomerular capillaries is high mainly because:
o: The afferent arteriole is narrower than the efferent arteriole
The glomerulus is connected directly to the aorta
The glomerular capillaries have thick muscular walls
The efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole
x: A wide afferent arteriole brings blood in, while a narrower efferent arteriole resists its exit, so pressure builds up in the glomerulus and drives filtration.

q: Which statement correctly compares the two capillary beds of a nephron?
o: Glomerular capillaries reabsorb; peritubular capillaries filter
Glomerular capillaries filter fluid out of the blood; peritubular capillaries take up reabsorbed substances
Both mainly filter fluid out of the blood
x: The glomerular bed is for filtration, while the peritubular bed around the tubules collects reabsorbed water and solutes and supplies substances for secretion.

q: The low hydrostatic pressure in the peritubular capillaries is useful because it:
o: Forces more filtrate out into the tubules
Prevents oxygen reaching the tubule cells
Allows reabsorbed fluid from the tubules to enter the blood easily
x: Low pressure (together with the high protein concentration of this blood) favours movement of fluid into the capillaries, so reabsorbed water and solutes are taken up.

q: Glomerular capillaries are unusual because they:
o: Lie between two arterioles instead of between an arteriole and a venule
Carry blood directly into the renal vein
Have no blood flowing through them
Are found only in the medulla
x: The glomerulus is fed by the afferent arteriole and drained by the efferent arteriole, an arteriole–capillary–arteriole arrangement that helps keep its pressure high.

q: Compared with blood in the afferent arteriole, blood in the efferent arteriole has:
o: A lower concentration of plasma proteins
A higher concentration of plasma proteins
x: Filtration removes water and small solutes but not proteins, so the proteins left in the efferent blood are more concentrated.

q: Blood from the peritubular capillaries drains into:
o: Venules that lead to the renal vein
x: Peritubular capillaries join to form venules, which lead into the renal vein and then the inferior vena cava.

q: Unlike most capillaries, the glomerular capillaries do not take fluid back in at their far end. Why?
o: They have no pores in their walls
Their pressure stays high along their whole length because the narrow efferent arteriole holds it up
Blood flows through them in both directions
x: In ordinary capillaries pressure falls along the vessel so fluid returns at the venous end. In the glomerulus the narrow efferent arteriole keeps pressure high throughout, so net movement is outward.

q: Substances secreted into the tubule, such as H+ ions and some drugs, come from blood in the:
x: Tubule cells take these substances from the peritubular capillary blood around them and pass them into the tubule fluid.

q: The walls of the glomerular capillaries have many pores (fenestrations). This feature:
o: Allows red blood cells to enter the filtrate
Allows rapid filtration of water and small solutes
Prevents any fluid from leaving the blood
x: Pores make the capillary wall very permeable to water and small solutes, so filtration is fast. Cells and large proteins are still held back.

q: Which pair of conditions in the peritubular capillaries favours the uptake of reabsorbed fluid?
o: Low hydrostatic pressure and high protein (osmotic) concentration
High hydrostatic pressure and low protein concentration
High hydrostatic pressure and high protein concentration
Low hydrostatic pressure and no plasma proteins
x: After filtration, peritubular blood has low pressure and concentrated proteins. Low pressure pushes little fluid out, while the proteins' osmotic pull draws fluid in.

q: Hydrostatic pressure in the peritubular capillaries is much lower than in the glomerulus partly because:
o: They are fed directly by the renal vein
Blood has passed through the narrow, resistant efferent arteriole
They have thicker walls than the glomerulus
x: The narrow efferent arteriole resists flow, so pressure drops as blood passes through it into the peritubular network.

q: A sharp fall in a person's general blood pressure, as after severe blood loss, would reduce the glomerular filtration rate because:
o: Plasma proteins would pass into the filtrate
The peritubular capillaries would start filtering
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure, the force driving filtration, would fall
x: Filtration depends on blood pressure in the glomerulus. If general blood pressure falls, glomerular pressure falls and less filtrate is formed.

q: The cells of the kidney tubules receive most of their oxygen and nutrients from the:
x: The peritubular capillaries surround the tubules and supply the tubule cells with oxygen and nutrients, as well as collecting what they reabsorb.

q: What is the correct order of blood flow through a nephron's blood supply?
o: Renal artery → efferent arteriole → glomerulus → afferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries → renal vein
Renal artery → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries → renal vein
Renal artery → peritubular capillaries → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → renal vein
Renal vein → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries → renal artery
x: Blood reaches the glomerulus by the afferent arteriole, leaves by the efferent arteriole, flows through the peritubular capillaries and finally drains to the renal vein.

q: Which is NOT a feature of the glomerular capillaries?
o: They take up the substances reabsorbed from the PCT
Their blood is at high hydrostatic pressure
They lie between the afferent and efferent arterioles
x: Reabsorbed substances from the PCT enter the peritubular capillaries, not the glomerulus. The other statements are true of glomerular capillaries.

q: In the cortex, the peritubular capillaries form a network mainly around the:
x: In the cortex the peritubular network wraps around the convoluted tubules, where most reabsorption and secretion take place.

q: Glucose reabsorbed by the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule passes next into the:
x: PCT cells move glucose out of their base into the tissue fluid, and it enters the surrounding peritubular capillaries to return to the circulation.

q: In a nephron's blood supply, how many capillary networks does blood pass through before it enters a renal venule?
x: Blood passes first through the glomerular capillaries and then through the peritubular capillaries (or vasa recta) before reaching a venule.

q: Blood entering the efferent arteriole has lost mainly:
o: Red blood cells and plasma proteins
Water and small solutes that formed the filtrate
All of its glucose by active transport
x: In the glomerulus, water and small solutes are filtered out; cells and proteins remain. The glomerulus is not where glucose is reabsorbed.

q: Blood in the vasa recta flows down into the medulla and back up again beside the loop of Henle. How does this help the kidney?
o: It filters extra plasma into the loop of Henle
It removes all the salt from the medulla
It carries urine to the renal pelvis
Solutes picked up on the way down are given back on the way up, so the medullary salt gradient is not washed away
x: The vasa recta act as a countercurrent exchanger: they supply the medulla with blood while returning salt to it on the ascending side, so the high medullary concentration is preserved.

q: Which statement is correct?
o: Glomerular capillaries have a higher hydrostatic pressure than peritubular capillaries
Peritubular capillaries arise from the afferent arteriole
The vasa recta lie inside Bowman's capsule
Glomerular capillaries drain directly into the renal vein
x: Glomerular pressure is high for filtration; peritubular pressure is low for reabsorption. Peritubular capillaries come from the efferent arteriole, and the glomerulus drains into the efferent arteriole.

q: If disease made the glomerular capillaries leaky to plasma proteins, which change would be expected?
o: Protein would appear in the urine
Glucose would no longer be filtered
The peritubular capillaries would start filtering
x: Normally proteins are held back by the glomerular filter. If it becomes leaky, proteins pass into the filtrate and appear in urine, as they are not reabsorbed in large amounts.

q: Which pair of changes would both increase the glomerular filtration rate?
o: Constriction of the afferent arteriole and dilation of the efferent arteriole
Constriction of both the afferent arteriole and the renal artery
Dilation of the afferent arteriole and constriction of the efferent arteriole
Dilation of the efferent arteriole and a fall in blood pressure
x: A wider afferent arteriole lets more blood in, and a narrower efferent arteriole holds it back; both raise glomerular pressure and so increase filtration.

q: Some drugs, such as penicillin, are removed from the blood faster than filtration alone could achieve. Which capillary bed makes this possible?
o: The glomerular capillaries, by filtering them twice
The vasa recta, by pumping them into Bowman's capsule
The renal vein, by returning them to the glomerulus
The peritubular capillaries, which deliver them to tubule cells for secretion
x: Drug molecules left in the blood after filtration reach the tubule cells through the peritubular capillaries, and the cells secrete them into the tubule fluid.

q: Compared with blood in the renal artery, blood in the renal vein of a healthy person contains:
x: The kidneys remove urea from the blood, so blood leaving in the renal vein has less urea than blood arriving in the renal artery.

q: Among the following, the highest hydrostatic blood pressure is found in the:
x: Glomerular capillaries are a high-pressure bed for filtration. Pressure is much lower in the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta, and lowest in the venules.

q: Which pairing of a kidney structure with its countercurrent role is correct?
o: Loop of Henle – countercurrent exchanger; vasa recta – countercurrent multiplier
Glomerulus – countercurrent multiplier; PCT – countercurrent exchanger
Collecting duct – countercurrent multiplier; renal vein – countercurrent exchanger
Loop of Henle – countercurrent multiplier; vasa recta – countercurrent exchanger
x: The loop of Henle builds the medullary gradient (multiplier), while the vasa recta maintain it without washing it out (exchanger).

q: The most common type of kidney stone in humans is made of:
x: Most kidney stones are calcium stones, and calcium oxalate is by far the commonest kind. Uric acid, cystine and struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones occur but are less frequent.

q: Kidney stones are also known as:
x: A stone (calculus) formed in the kidney is a renal calculus. Cysts are fluid-filled sacs, not hard mineral deposits.

q: Kidney stones form mainly because:
o: Salts in concentrated urine crystallise and the crystals grow
Bacteria multiply and harden inside the nephron
Blood clots collect in the renal pelvis
Fat is deposited in the walls of the collecting ducts
x: When urine holds more of a salt than can stay dissolved, the salt crystallises; the crystals stick together and grow into a stone. Clots, fat and bacteria are not the basis of stones.

q: Which everyday habit most directly raises the risk of kidney stones?
x: Low water intake makes urine small in volume and concentrated, so dissolved salts reach the level at which they crystallise. Fibre, sleep position and exercise do not cause stones.

q: Uric acid kidney stones are commonly associated with:
x: In gout the level of uric acid in the blood is high, so more uric acid enters the urine and can precipitate as stones. Anaemia, diabetes insipidus and hypothyroidism are not the classic link.

q: Struvite stones are chemically made of:
x: Struvite is magnesium ammonium phosphate. These stones are linked to urinary tract infections. Calcium oxalate and uric acid form other stone types.

q: In shock-wave lithotripsy, a kidney stone is treated by:
o: Dissolving it with acid injected into the kidney
Freezing it so that it shrinks
Breaking it into small pieces with shock waves from outside the body
x: Lithotripsy focuses high-energy shock (sound) waves on the stone from outside the body. The stone breaks into fragments small enough to pass out with urine.

q: The word 'lithotripsy' literally means:
x: 'Litho' means stone and 'tripsy' means crushing or rubbing. Lithotripsy is the crushing of stones into small pieces.

q: A main advantage of shock-wave lithotripsy over open surgery for kidney stones is that:
o: No incision in the body is needed
It works on stones of every size
It removes the stone in one solid piece
x: The shock waves are given from outside the body, so no cut is made. Very large stones may still need surgery, stones can form again, and the stone leaves as fragments, not whole.

q: After successful lithotripsy, the fragments of a kidney stone usually leave the body:
o: Through the blood to the liver
x: The small fragments travel down the ureter to the bladder and are passed out in urine. They do not enter the blood or the gut.

q: A very large kidney stone that cannot be broken down by lithotripsy is usually treated by:
x: Large stones that shock waves cannot break are removed surgically, either by open surgery or by keyhole methods. Dialysis and transplant are treatments for kidney failure, not for stones.

q: In keyhole (percutaneous) surgery for a kidney stone, the stone is removed:
o: By a large cut across the abdomen
By passing it through the blood
Through a small incision in the back using a narrow tube
x: In percutaneous surgery a small cut is made in the back and a narrow tube with an instrument is passed into the kidney to break up and remove the stone. Open surgery uses a large incision.

q: Overactivity of the parathyroid glands raises blood calcium. Such a person is more likely to form:
o: No stones, as calcium prevents stones
x: Excess parathyroid hormone releases calcium from bone, so more calcium appears in the urine and can precipitate as calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate stones.

q: A diet very rich in oxalate-containing foods such as spinach most directly increases the risk of:
x: Oxalate from food is excreted in urine, where it combines with calcium to form insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Struvite stones are linked to infection, and uric acid stones to uric acid levels.

q: A diet very high in meat and other animal protein most directly raises the risk of:
x: Such foods are rich in purines, whose breakdown gives uric acid. More uric acid in urine favours uric acid stones. Struvite stones follow infection, and the other two are not stones.

q: A stone moving from the kidney down the ureter typically causes:
o: High fever with shivering in every case
Severe pain in the back or side that spreads towards the groin
x: The stone stretches and irritates the narrow ureter as it moves, causing severe colicky pain from the back or side towards the groin, often with blood in the urine.

q: A kidney stone most often gets stuck while passing through the:
x: The ureter is a narrow tube from the kidney to the bladder, so stones often lodge in it. Stones do not travel through blood vessels or the glomerulus.

q: Blood in the urine of a person with a kidney stone is usually because:
o: The stone dissolves red blood cells
The rough stone scratches the lining of the urinary tract
x: Stones have rough, sharp edges that damage the lining of the renal pelvis, ureter or bladder as they move, so a little blood enters the urine.

q: Which of the following is NOT a type of kidney stone?
x: Sodium chloride is very soluble and is excreted dissolved in urine, so it does not form stones. Calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate and uric acid are all recognised stone types.

q: Which of the following does NOT increase the risk of kidney stone formation?
x: Plenty of water keeps urine dilute, so salts stay dissolved; it lowers the risk. Infection, high oxalate and dehydration all favour stones.

q: Drinking more water helps prevent kidney stones because it:
o: Keeps urine dilute so salts stay below the level at which they crystallise
Makes the kidneys produce less urine
Stops the liver from making urea
x: More water means a larger volume of more dilute urine. Stone-forming salts then stay dissolved instead of crystallising.

q: Kidney stones are more common in hot climates mainly because people there:
o: Lose much water in sweat and pass more concentrated urine
x: Heavy sweating removes water, so if intake is not increased the urine becomes concentrated and salts crystallise more easily.

q: A stone completely blocking the ureter of one kidney can lead to:
o: More urine being made by that kidney
Urine backing up so that kidney swells and may be damaged
Urine passing directly into the blood
x: A blocked ureter stops urine draining, so it backs up into the kidney, which swells and can lose function if the blockage is not relieved. Stones are thus also a cause of kidney damage.

q: Which statement about shock-wave lithotripsy is correct?
o: The waves are focused on the stone so it breaks while nearby tissue is little harmed
It is used to clean the blood of urea
It can only be done during open surgery
x: The shock waves are aimed so that their energy is concentrated at the stone, breaking it, while the tissues they pass through receive much less. No donor or open surgery is involved.

q: A kidney stone is made mainly of:
x: Kidney stones are hard masses of crystallised salts such as calcium oxalate, with a little organic material binding them. They are not clots, fat or simply bacteria.

q: The treatment that uses shock waves to break kidney stones is called:
x: Lithotripsy breaks stones with shock waves. Dialysis treats kidney failure, angioplasty widens blood vessels and nephrectomy is removal of a kidney.

q: Uric acid stones are most likely to form when urine is:
x: Uric acid is poorly soluble, and least soluble in acidic urine, so concentrated acidic urine favours its crystals. Dilute or alkaline urine keeps more uric acid dissolved.

q: A patient has repeated urinary infections with bacteria that split urea into ammonia. The urine becomes alkaline. Which stones are these conditions known to favour?
o: No stones, as alkaline urine dissolves all salts
x: Ammonia from urea makes the urine alkaline and supplies ammonium ions, so magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) precipitates. Uric acid stones favour acidic urine instead.

q: A person excretes the same daily amount of calcium oxalate but doubles their urine volume. The risk of calcium oxalate stones will:
o: Fall, as the salt is now at half the concentration
Double, as more urine passes the kidney
Stay the same, as the amount of salt is unchanged
Rise, as the urine becomes more acidic
x: Crystals form when concentration is too high, not simply when the amount is large. The same amount in twice the volume is half as concentrated, so it is less likely to crystallise.

q: Which is the correct order of events in kidney stone disease?
o: Urine becomes concentrated, crystals form, crystals grow into a stone, stone moves into the ureter
Stone blocks ureter, urine becomes concentrated, crystals form, crystals grow
Crystals grow, crystals form, urine becomes concentrated, stone blocks ureter
Crystals form, stone moves into the ureter, urine becomes concentrated, crystals grow
x: Salts first reach a high concentration, then crystallise; the crystals grow into a stone, which may later move into and block the ureter, causing pain.

q: Which statement about kidney stone treatment is NOT correct?
o: Small stones may pass out in the urine on their own
Lithotripsy removes the stone through a cut in the back
Large stones may need surgical removal
x: Lithotripsy uses shock waves from outside the body and needs no cut; removal through a small cut in the back is keyhole surgery. The other three statements are correct.

q: A small kidney stone of a few millimetres often:
o: Passes out with the urine without surgery
x: Small stones can travel down the ureter and be passed in urine, helped by good fluid intake. Larger stones need lithotripsy or surgery.

q: Kidney failure is best described as a condition in which the kidneys:
o: Can no longer remove wastes and balance water and salts properly
x: In kidney failure the kidneys cannot adequately clear wastes such as urea or keep water and salt balance. Kidneys do not make urea; the liver does.

q: The machine used in haemodialysis is often called:
x: The dialyser cleans the blood outside the body in place of the kidneys, so it is called an artificial kidney.

q: Which statement correctly compares acute and chronic kidney failure?
o: Acute failure develops slowly over many years
Chronic failure always recovers fully within days
Both types always follow kidney stones
Acute failure develops suddenly and may recover; chronic failure develops gradually and is usually permanent
x: Acute failure comes on over hours or days, often from a sudden cause, and may be reversed. Chronic failure is a slow, progressive loss of nephrons that usually cannot be reversed.

q: The two commonest causes of chronic kidney failure are:
o: Diabetes mellitus and high blood pressure
x: Long-standing high blood glucose and high blood pressure both slowly damage the glomeruli and small blood vessels of the kidney.

q: After a road accident with heavy bleeding, a person's urine output falls sharply. The likely cause is:
o: Acute kidney failure due to reduced blood flow to the kidneys
x: Severe blood loss lowers blood pressure, so too little blood reaches the glomeruli to be filtered. This is a classic sudden (acute) cause.

q: A blood test that would suggest kidney failure is:
x: Failing kidneys cannot excrete urea and creatinine, so these wastes build up in the blood. Low levels would point the other way.

q: In haemodialysis, the dialysis fluid contains:
o: A higher urea concentration than blood
No urea, with glucose and salts at about normal blood levels
Red blood cells to replace those lost
x: With no urea in the fluid, urea diffuses out of the blood. Glucose and salts are kept at normal plasma levels so the blood does not lose the useful amounts it should keep.

q: Why does the dialysis fluid contain glucose at the same concentration as normal blood plasma?
o: So that glucose diffuses into the blood to feed the patient
So that urea combines with glucose
So that the membrane does not let glucose through
So that there is no net loss of glucose from the blood
x: With equal glucose concentrations on both sides there is no concentration gradient, so no net glucose diffuses out. The membrane itself does let small molecules like glucose through.

q: The membrane separating blood from dialysis fluid in a dialyser is:
o: Partially permeable, letting small molecules pass but not blood cells and plasma proteins
x: Small molecules such as urea, salts and glucose can cross; large proteins and blood cells cannot, so they stay in the blood.

q: During haemodialysis, heparin is added to the patient's blood in order to:
o: Prevent the blood from clotting in the machine
Kill bacteria in the dialysis fluid
x: Heparin is an anticoagulant. Without it, blood would clot in the tubes and dialyser.

q: In a dialyser, blood and dialysis fluid flow in opposite directions. This is done to:
o: Allow red cells to cross the membrane
Keep a concentration gradient for urea along the whole length of the membrane
x: In counter-current flow the blood always meets fluid with less urea than itself, so urea keeps diffusing out along the whole membrane. Flow in the same direction would let the two sides reach balance.

q: In peritoneal dialysis, the membrane through which wastes pass is:
o: The patient's own peritoneum lining the abdominal cavity
A plastic tube in a machine
The wall of the urinary bladder
x: Dialysis fluid is placed in the abdominal cavity, and wastes diffuse out of blood vessels in the peritoneum into it. The peritoneum acts as the dialysis membrane.

q: In peritoneal dialysis, the dialysis fluid is put into the patient's:
x: Fluid is run into the abdominal (peritoneal) cavity through a catheter, left for some hours to collect wastes, then drained and replaced.

q: Which statement about peritoneal dialysis is correct?
o: It can be done at home, and the patient can move about during it
The blood leaves the body and passes through a machine
It uses heparin in large amounts every time
x: Because the patient's own peritoneum is used and the fluid simply runs in and out through a catheter, it can be done at home and the patient can stay mobile. In haemodialysis the blood passes through a machine.

q: The main problem after a kidney transplant is:
o: The new kidney producing too much urine
Rejection of the donor kidney by the patient's immune system
The new kidney forming stones at once
x: The immune system may recognise the donor kidney's cells as foreign and attack them. This rejection is the main risk after a transplant.

q: The risk of rejection after a kidney transplant is reduced by:
o: Close tissue matching and immunosuppressive drugs
x: Choosing a donor whose tissue type closely matches the patient and giving drugs that suppress the immune system both lower the chance of rejection.

q: Rejection of a transplanted kidney is least likely when the donor is the patient's:
x: Identical twins have the same genes and the same tissue antigens, so the immune system does not see the kidney as foreign. Other people match less closely.

q: Patients taking immunosuppressive drugs after a kidney transplant are more likely to:
x: These drugs reduce the activity of the immune system to prevent rejection, but this also weakens the body's defence against infections.

q: How can kidney stones lead to kidney failure?
o: By blocking urine flow so that pressure builds up and damages the kidney
By stopping the liver from making urea
x: A stone blocking urine outflow causes urine to back up, and the rising pressure damages the kidney tissue. Obstruction is one recognised cause of kidney failure.

q: Inflammation of the glomeruli, often following an infection, is called:
x: Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli and is an important cause of kidney failure. Nephrolithiasis means kidney stones, hydronephrosis is swelling from blocked urine, and hepatitis affects the liver.

q: Long-standing diabetes mellitus can cause kidney failure mainly because:
o: Insulin is made in the kidney
Glucose forms stones in the ureter
High blood glucose damages the glomerular capillaries over the years
x: Years of high blood glucose damage the small blood vessels of the glomeruli, so filtration gradually fails. Insulin is made in the pancreas, not the kidney.

q: Long-standing high blood pressure can lead to kidney failure because it:
o: Increases urea production in the liver
Damages the blood vessels and glomeruli of the kidney
x: Persistently high pressure damages the walls of the renal blood vessels and glomeruli, and nephrons are slowly lost.

q: Swelling of the body (oedema) in kidney failure occurs because:
o: The kidneys excrete too much water
Water and salt are retained in the body
Blood cells leak into the tissues
x: Failing kidneys cannot excrete enough water and salt, so the extra fluid collects in the tissues and causes swelling.

q: Large amounts of protein in the urine suggest kidney damage because:
o: Healthy glomeruli do not let most plasma proteins pass, so the filter must be damaged
Proteins are normally made in the kidney
Proteins are always reabsorbed in the bladder
x: Plasma proteins are too large to pass a healthy glomerular filter. Their presence in urine means the filtration barrier is damaged.

q: Which can damage kidney tubules and cause acute kidney failure?
o: Certain poisons and some drugs in high doses
x: Some toxic chemicals and certain medicines taken in large doses damage the tubule cells and can cause sudden kidney failure.

q: During haemodialysis, which substance passes from the blood into the dialysis fluid?
x: Urea is a small molecule that diffuses down its concentration gradient into the urea-free dialysis fluid. Cells and proteins are too large to cross the membrane.

q: If the dialysis fluid contained a higher sodium concentration than the patient's blood, then during dialysis:
o: Sodium would diffuse from the blood into the fluid
Sodium would diffuse from the fluid into the blood
No sodium would move because ions cannot cross
Urea would stop leaving the blood
x: Small ions such as sodium cross the membrane and diffuse from higher to lower concentration, so sodium would enter the blood. Urea removal depends on its own gradient and would continue.

q: Which statement about dialysis and kidney transplant is correct?
o: Dialysis must be repeated regularly, while a working transplant restores kidney function
Dialysis cures kidney failure after one session
A transplant needs no further medicine
Neither can keep a patient alive
x: Dialysis only removes wastes for a time, so it must be repeated. A successful transplant takes over kidney function, though drugs are still needed to prevent rejection.

q: An inherited condition in which many fluid-filled cysts grow in both kidneys, slowly destroying them, is:
x: In polycystic kidney disease the cysts gradually replace normal tissue, a genetic cause of chronic kidney failure.

q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of acute kidney failure?
o: Severe blood loss after an injury
Sudden blockage of urine flow by a stone
Slow damage from many years of diabetes
x: Damage from long-standing diabetes builds up over years and causes chronic failure. The other three act suddenly and are causes of acute failure.

q: In haemodialysis, the used dialysis fluid is continuously replaced with fresh fluid so that:
o: Urea does not build up in the fluid, so it keeps diffusing out of the blood
x: If the fluid were not replaced, its urea concentration would rise until it matched the blood and diffusion would stop. Fresh fluid keeps the gradient.

q: Compared with haemodialysis, in peritoneal dialysis:
o: The blood is pumped through an external dialyser
The blood stays inside the body
x: Peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneum inside the abdomen as the membrane, so the blood never leaves the body. In haemodialysis blood passes through a dialyser outside the body.

q: Thermoregulation is the process of:
o: Regulating the amount of water in blood
Keeping body temperature within narrow limits
x: Thermoregulation keeps the core body temperature within a narrow range. Water balance is osmoregulation, and removing nitrogenous wastes is excretion.

q: The part of the human brain that acts as the body's thermostat is the:
x: The hypothalamus monitors body temperature and switches on heat-loss or heat-gain responses. The cerebellum coordinates movement.

q: Body temperature must be kept fairly constant mainly because:
o: Blood freezes just below body temperature
Enzymes work best at an optimum temperature and are denatured if it gets too high
Water cannot be absorbed at other temperatures
x: Metabolism depends on enzymes. Below the optimum they work slowly, and too much heat denatures them, so temperature control keeps reactions steady.

q: Ectotherms are animals that:
o: Produce most of their body heat by metabolism
Keep a constant body temperature in all conditions
Never change their behaviour with temperature
Get most of their body heat from the environment
x: Ectotherms rely on outside heat, so their body temperature varies with the environment, though they can adjust it by behaviour. Endotherms produce most of their heat by metabolism.

q: Which groups of animals are endotherms?
x: Birds and mammals generate most of their body heat internally and keep a fairly constant temperature. Fishes, amphibians, reptiles and insects are ectotherms.

q: Which of the following animals is an ectotherm?
x: Lizards are reptiles and depend on outside heat. Pigeons, bats and whales are birds or mammals, which are endotherms.

q: Compared with an ectotherm of the same size, an endotherm:
o: Needs much more food because of its high metabolic rate
Must bask in the sun before it can move
x: Endotherms burn food at a high rate to make heat, so they need far more food. Becoming sluggish in cold and basking are features of ectotherms.

q: A lizard lies on a sunny rock in the early morning. This is an example of:
o: Behavioural regulation to raise body temperature
x: Ectotherms like lizards control body temperature largely by behaviour. Basking absorbs heat from the sun to warm the body before activity.

q: Sweating cools the body because:
o: Sweat is colder than the skin
Evaporation of water from the skin takes heat from the body
Sweat blocks heat production in muscles
x: Changing liquid water to vapour needs heat (latent heat of vaporisation), which is taken from the skin and so cools the body.

q: Sweating cools the body less well on a hot, humid day because:
o: Less sweat is produced in humid air
Air already full of water vapour slows evaporation of sweat
x: Cooling depends on sweat evaporating. When the air is nearly saturated with water vapour, evaporation is slow, so sweat drips off without removing much heat.

q: On a hot day the skin looks flushed because:
o: Arterioles in the skin dilate, bringing more blood near the surface
x: Vasodilation of skin arterioles sends more warm blood close to the surface, where heat is lost by radiation, making the skin look red.

q: In cold conditions, vasoconstriction of skin arterioles helps by:
o: Increasing heat loss from the skin
Reducing blood flow near the surface so less heat is lost
Raising the water content of blood
x: Narrowed skin arterioles carry less blood to the surface, so less heat escapes. This is why skin looks pale in the cold.

q: Shivering helps raise body temperature because:
o: It reduces blood flow to the brain
Rapid involuntary contractions of skeletal muscles release heat
It stops the heart from beating fast
x: Shivering is rapid, involuntary muscle contraction. The respiration that powers it releases heat, warming the body.

q: Hair erection in mammals in cold weather helps because:
o: It increases blood flow to the skin
Erect hairs trap a thicker layer of still air, which insulates the body
x: Contraction of the erector (arrector pili) muscles raises the hairs. The trapped still air is a poor conductor of heat. In humans this only gives goose bumps.

q: Fever occurs when:
o: Pyrogens raise the temperature set point of the hypothalamus
The body loses all its heat-producing ability
Blood vessels in the skin stay permanently dilated
x: Pyrogens act on the hypothalamus and reset its set point higher. The body then uses heat-gain responses to reach and hold this new, higher temperature.

q: Pyrogens that cause fever come from:
o: Bacteria or other microbes and chemicals released by white blood cells
x: Pyrogens are fever-producing substances. Some come from microbes, and some are released by the body's white blood cells during infection.

q: At the start of a fever, a person feels cold and shivers although body temperature is rising. This is because:
o: The body temperature is now below the new, higher set point
x: The hypothalamus now compares body temperature with a higher set point, so the body seems too cold and heat-gain responses such as shivering and vasoconstriction start.

q: When a fever 'breaks' and the set point returns to normal, the person typically:
o: Sweats and the skin becomes flushed
x: The body is now warmer than the normal set point, so heat-loss responses start: sweating and vasodilation of skin arterioles.

q: A mild fever may help the body because:
o: It denatures the body's own enzymes
It stops the heart from pumping
It may slow the growth of some microbes and help the immune response
x: A moderately raised temperature can slow the multiplication of some pathogens and help the defence responses. Very high fever is harmful.

q: A very high fever is dangerous mainly because:
o: Body proteins and enzymes may be denatured
The kidneys make too much urine
Blood becomes too acidic to clot
x: Too much heat changes the shape of proteins, including enzymes, so they stop working. This can damage cells, especially in the brain.

q: In long-term cold, which hormone raises the metabolic rate and so increases heat production?
x: Thyroxine from the thyroid gland raises the metabolic rate of cells, producing more heat. ADH controls water reabsorption, and insulin and glucagon control blood glucose.

q: Brown fat in newborn babies and hibernating mammals is important because it:
x: Brown fat is specialised to release the energy of its stored fat as heat. This non-shivering heat production warms newborns and animals arousing from hibernation.

q: On a very hot day the air temperature rises above body temperature. The body can then lose heat only by:
o: Evaporation of sweat from the skin
Radiation of heat from the skin
Conduction of heat to the surrounding air
Convection currents in the air around the skin
x: Radiation, conduction and convection move heat only from a warmer to a cooler object, so when the air is hotter than the skin the body gains heat by these routes. Evaporation of sweat still removes heat, so it becomes the only way of cooling.

q: In the legs of some birds living in cold places, warm arterial blood heats cold venous blood returning to the body. This arrangement:
o: Reduces heat loss by keeping heat in the body core
Increases heat loss from the feet
Makes the feet warmer than the body
x: In this counter-current heat exchange, heat passes from outgoing arterial blood to returning venous blood, so little reaches the feet to be lost to the cold.

q: A dog pants on a hot day. Panting cools it mainly by:
o: Evaporation of water from the moist surfaces of the mouth and airways
Making its hair stand on end
x: Rapid shallow breathing passes air over moist surfaces, and evaporation of that water removes heat. Dogs have few sweat glands in their skin.

q: Animals such as bats and hummingbirds, which keep a high body temperature when active but let it fall when resting, are called:
x: Heterotherms regulate their temperature like endotherms at some times and let it drop at others, saving energy.

q: Which response would NOT occur when a person enters a very cold room?
x: Sweating removes heat, so it decreases in the cold. Vasoconstriction, shivering and hair erection all conserve or produce heat.

q: Normal human core body temperature is about:
x: The human core temperature is kept close to 37 °C. A temperature of 40 °C or more is a high fever.

q: The hypothalamus detects changes in body temperature by:
o: Receptors that sense the temperature of blood, plus signals from skin receptors
Detecting light falling on the skin
x: Cells in the hypothalamus monitor the temperature of blood flowing through it, and temperature receptors in the skin send it information about the surroundings.

q: Thermoregulation is an example of negative feedback because:
o: A change in temperature is made larger
A change in temperature causes responses that reverse that change
x: In negative feedback the response opposes the change: a rise in temperature triggers cooling, and a fall triggers warming, returning it towards the set point.

q: A man in a hot desert becomes so dehydrated that he stops sweating. His body temperature will most probably:
o: Rise, as the main way of losing heat by evaporation is lost
Fall, as less water is lost
Stay the same, as vasodilation fully replaces sweating
x: In hot surroundings evaporation of sweat is the main cooling route. Without it heat builds up, so body temperature rises, which can lead to heat stroke.

q: A small mammal loses body heat faster than a large one in the same cold place mainly because it has:
o: A smaller surface area to volume ratio
A larger surface area to volume ratio
x: Heat is lost through the surface. A small animal has more surface for each unit of heat-producing volume, so it cools faster and needs a higher metabolic rate.

q: Which nitrogenous waste is the most toxic?
x: Ammonia is highly toxic even at low concentration. Urea is much less toxic and uric acid is the least toxic of the three main wastes.

q: The main nitrogenous waste excreted by humans is:
x: Humans and other mammals are ureotelic: most excess nitrogen leaves as urea in urine. Only small amounts of uric acid and ammonia are excreted.

q: Birds excrete their nitrogenous waste mainly as:
x: Birds are uricotelic. Uric acid is nearly insoluble and is passed as a white paste with very little water.

q: Ammonia can be the main nitrogenous waste of bony fishes and many aquatic invertebrates because:
o: They live in water, which quickly dilutes and carries away the ammonia
They have no kidneys or gills
x: Ammonia is toxic and needs a lot of water to dilute it. Animals living in water can release it continuously into their surroundings, mainly by diffusion.

q: Excreting uric acid suits animals that develop inside a shelled egg because uric acid:
o: Turns into water in the egg
Is insoluble and non-toxic, so it can be stored safely inside the egg
Is removed by the mother's blood
x: An embryo inside a shelled egg cannot get rid of wastes, so they must be stored. Insoluble, non-toxic uric acid crystals can be stored without harming it.

q: The correct order of nitrogenous wastes, from the MOST water needed for excretion to the LEAST, is:
x: Ammonia must be heavily diluted, urea needs a moderate amount of water and insoluble uric acid needs very little.

q: In mammals, urea is made in the:
x: Liver cells convert ammonia into urea by the ornithine cycle. The kidneys only remove urea from the blood.

q: In the liver, ammonia is produced from excess amino acids by:
x: Deamination removes the amino group of an amino acid as ammonia. The remaining part can be used for energy or turned into glucose or fat.

q: In the ornithine cycle, ornithine first combines with ammonia and carbon dioxide (carried as carbamoyl phosphate) to form:
x: Ornithine plus ammonia and carbon dioxide gives citrulline. Citrulline then gains another amino group to become arginine, which is split to give urea.

q: Which is the correct order of compounds in the ornithine cycle?
o: Ornithine, arginine, citrulline, urea and ornithine
Citrulline, ornithine, arginine, urea and citrulline
Ornithine, citrulline, arginine, urea and ornithine
Arginine, ornithine, citrulline, urea and arginine
x: Ornithine becomes citrulline, citrulline becomes arginine, and arginine is split into urea and ornithine, which starts the cycle again.

q: In the ornithine cycle, the enzyme that splits arginine into urea and ornithine is:
x: Arginase hydrolyses arginine to urea and ornithine. Urease is a different enzyme, found in some bacteria, that breaks urea down into ammonia and carbon dioxide.

q: The ornithine cycle is also known as the:
x: It is called the urea cycle because its product is urea. The Krebs cycle is part of aerobic respiration, and the Calvin cycle is part of photosynthesis.

q: Which statement about the formation of urea is correct?
o: It releases a large amount of energy
It happens in the kidney tubules
It needs energy in the form of ATP
x: Converting ammonia to urea in the ornithine cycle uses ATP. It is controlled by enzymes and takes place in the liver.

q: Creatinine is a nitrogenous waste formed from:
o: Breakdown of creatine phosphate in muscles
x: Muscles use creatine phosphate as a quick energy store; its breakdown gives creatinine, which the kidneys excrete in urine.

q: Doctors measure the creatinine level in blood mainly to:
o: Check how well the kidneys are working
x: Creatinine is made at a fairly steady rate and removed by the kidneys, so a rise in blood creatinine suggests that kidney function has fallen.

q: A tadpole excretes mainly ammonia, but the adult frog excretes mainly urea. This change is linked to:
o: The adult living only in water
The adult spending much time on land, where water must be conserved
x: In water the tadpole can lose toxic ammonia easily. The adult frog lives partly on land, so it changes to urea, which is less toxic and needs less water.

q: Which group of animals is mainly uricotelic?
x: Insects, like birds, reptiles and land snails, excrete mainly uric acid, saving water. Bony fishes and tadpoles excrete ammonia, and mammals excrete urea.

q: In humans, uric acid is mainly formed from the breakdown of:
x: Purine bases of nucleic acids are broken down to uric acid. Fats and sugars contain no nitrogen and cannot form nitrogenous waste.

q: Gout is a condition in which:
o: Urea crystals form in the liver
Ammonia builds up in the gills
Uric acid crystals collect in joints, causing painful inflammation
x: In gout blood uric acid is high, and crystals of uric acid (as urate) are deposited in joints, which become inflamed and painful.

q: Ammonia is not stored in the body of land animals because it:
o: Is highly toxic even at low concentrations
x: Ammonia is very toxic, so land animals convert it quickly into less toxic urea or uric acid rather than letting it build up.

q: In bony fishes, most ammonia leaves the body:
o: By diffusion across the gills into the water
x: Ammonia is very soluble and diffuses out across the gill surfaces into the surrounding water.

q: Which statement about nitrogenous wastes is NOT correct?
o: Ammonia is more toxic than urea
Urea is made in the liver
Birds and reptiles excrete mainly uric acid
Uric acid needs more water for excretion than urea
x: Uric acid is nearly insoluble and needs the least water of all; urea needs more. The other three statements are correct.

q: Of the three main nitrogenous wastes, which takes the most energy to produce?
x: Ammonia comes straight from deamination at almost no cost; urea needs ATP in the ornithine cycle; uric acid is the most costly to make. Animals pay this cost in return for saving water.

q: Mammals excrete mainly urea rather than ammonia because urea:
o: Is less toxic and can be carried in blood and concentrated in urine
Is more toxic but needs less energy
Is insoluble and stored in eggs
Is a gas excreted through the lungs
x: Urea is fairly non-toxic and soluble, so it can travel safely in blood and be excreted in concentrated urine, saving water compared with ammonia.

q: Desert reptiles benefit from excreting uric acid mainly because:
o: It is more toxic than ammonia
It is made without any energy
It is used to make sweat
It is passed as a semi-solid paste, so very little water is lost
x: Uric acid precipitates and leaves as a paste, so water can be reabsorbed and little is lost, an advantage where water is scarce.

q: Nitrogenous wastes are produced mainly from the breakdown of:
x: Only nitrogen-containing molecules can yield nitrogenous waste: amino acids from proteins, and bases from nucleic acids. Carbohydrates and fats contain no nitrogen.

q: After urea is made in the liver, it reaches the kidneys:
o: In the bile through the gut
Inside red blood cells bound to haemoglobin
x: Urea is soluble, so it is carried dissolved in blood plasma to the kidneys, where it is filtered out into urine.

q: How many nitrogen atoms are present in one molecule of urea, CO(NH2)2?
x: Urea has two amino (NH2) groups joined to one carbonyl group, so each molecule carries two nitrogen atoms.

q: Which animal is correctly matched with its main nitrogenous waste?
x: Birds such as the pigeon are uricotelic. Humans excrete urea, bony fishes such as rohu excrete ammonia, and lizards excrete uric acid.

q: Marine sharks keep a high concentration of urea in their blood. This helps them because:
o: It makes their body fluids nearly as concentrated as sea water, reducing water loss by osmosis
x: Retained urea raises the solute concentration of shark blood close to that of sea water, so they do not lose water to the sea by osmosis.

q: Which of the following is NOT a nitrogenous waste?
x: Carbon dioxide is a waste of respiration but contains no nitrogen. Urea, creatinine and uric acid all contain nitrogen.
